newLeakNamedAndCut.name: REALM-TEARDOWN-RELEASE-HOST-COMMIT
newLeakNamedAndCut.mechanism: each panel Chart registers a closure on the HOST window (parentWin.addEventListener('talariaMcHostDataCommit', handler)). The closure captures the panel Chart, so the host pins the whole panel realm — script sources and compiled code included — after the iframe is removed. No removeEventListener for that event existed anywhere in chart.js.

nextRetainerNamed.name: HOST-BAR-CACHE-PINS-PANEL-REALM
nextRetainerNamed.path: object Object --property:put -> closure put --internal:context -> context files -> Map -> entry -> property tfs -> Map -> entry -> property bars -> Array -> element[0] -> a bar object -> __proto__ -> constructor -> the panel realm's NativeContext -> global_object
nextRetainerNamed.mechanism: the host bar cache (files -> tfs -> bars) stores plain objects that were ALLOCATED INSIDE a panel realm. Each such object's prototype and constructor belong to that realm, so ONE cached bar pins the entire realm — roughly 20MB of script sources and compiled code.
nextRetainerNamed.sameShapeAs: Chart._mcHostCacheFileRefOwners on deployed: a host cache holding a Map built in the panel realm. Two instances of one class of defect.
nextRetainerNamed.explainsPriorNullResult: this is why the ten cache shots in W74 (several of them caps) never moved the rate: capping bounds how MANY bars the cache holds, but a single surviving bar still pins a whole realm. The mass that matters is not the cache, it is the realm the cache reaches.
nextRetainerNamed.cutShape: either copy bars into host-realm objects on ingest (structuredClone or rebuild) so the cache never holds a foreign-realm object, or key the cache by realm and evict on removeChart
nextRetainerNamed.owner: product-side; A. Not mine to cut tonight and not behind my flags.
